title: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari

facts.claim: The book is a fable (fiction), copyright 1997. Narrator John, a lawyer, tells the story of his mentor Julian Mantle.
Julian, one of the country's most distinguished trial lawyers, known for three-thousand-dollar Italian suits, collapsed in the middle of a packed courtroom; the bailiff started CPR.

He worked eighteen-hour days; seven-figure income, a mansion, a private jet, a summer home on a tropical island and his prized possession, a shiny red Ferrari parked in the center of his driveway. He could not sleep more than a couple of hours without waking guilty about a file.
His marriage failed, he no longer spoke with his father; at fifty-three he looked as if he were in his late seventies. John had known him for seventeen years.
The massive heart attack came on a Monday morning in courtroom number seven, while he argued the Air Atlantic case, the same courtroom where they had won the 'Mother of All Murder Trials'.
His doctor's ultimatum: give up the Law or give up his life. He quit the firm, sold his mansion, his plane, his private island and even his Ferrari, and went to India.

A temple caretaker, Yogi Krishnan, told him of the Great Sages of Sivana high in the Himalayas ('Sivana' means 'oasis of enlightenment'); nobody knew where they lived. Julian climbed alone, without a Sherpa guide, and met Yogi Raman, the eldest sage.
After only three weeks in Sivana he began noticing beauty in ordinary things, a starry night, a spider's web after rain.

About three years after he left, a man who looked to be in his mid-thirties knocked at John's office and would not leave: 'Is this how you treat all of your visitors, John...?' It was Julian, lineless face, no cough.

Yogi Raman's fable: a garden, a six-story red lighthouse, a nine-foot, nine-hundred-pound sumo wrestler wearing a pink wire cable, a gold stopwatch, yellow roses, a path of diamonds. The seven elements are memory pegs for the sages' system.
John's father: 'John, on your deathbed you will never wish you spent more time at the office.' John then started spending a little more time at home.

About six months after Julian arrived, Divea, the youngest sage, brought him a gift from all the sages: a miniature hourglass of blown glass and a small piece of sandalwood. Each sage had received one as a child as a daily reminder of mortality.
The gold stopwatch symbolizes time; 'time slips through our hands like grains of sand'; everyone gets days of twenty-four hours.

Divea's advice: 'the best time to plant a tree was forty years ago. The second best time is today.' Julian: 'Develop a deathbed mentality': live every day as if it was your last; ask 'What would I do today if it was my last?'; you will start focusing on the meaningful things you have been putting off. John: 'Sounds kind of morbid.' Julian: it is a philosophy about life.
Chapter 11 techniques include the Ancient Rule of 20, Have the Courage to Say 'No', and the Deathbed Mentality.
facts.source: https://archive.org/details/TheMonkWhoSoldHisFerrariRobinS.Sharma (full text, HarperCollins ed.), ch. 11 Action Summary

facts.claim: The sumo wrestler symbolizes kaizen, which Yogi Raman says the great teachers of the ancient East developed centuries ago; 'This Japanese word means constant and never-ending improvement.' 'Self-mastery is the DNA of life mastery'; success on the outside begins within.

Julian tells John (215 pounds) to do push-ups until he can do no more. John stops at twenty-three. Julian: 'Do ten more.' John does ten. Yogi Raman did the same with Julian: 'pain was a great teacher'; people grow most in the 'Zone of the Unknown'; 'The only limits on your life are those that you set yourself.'
John then lists what he could improve: exercise, his nasty temper and habit of interrupting, his worry habit. Chapter 9 techniques: Do the Things You Fear; the 10 Ancient Rituals for Radiant Living.
Editorial: as a management term, kaizen reached Western business through Masaaki Imai's 1986 book and is tied to postwar Japanese industry; the 'centuries-old' origin is the fable's framing.

rejected.claim: Julian stayed years in a monastery.
rejected.reason: He lived with the Sages of Sivana in a mountain village; about three years passed before his return.

rejected.claim: Research on the dying listing five regrets (live my dream, work less, express feelings, friends, let myself be happy).
rejected.reason: Bronnie Ware's list (2009 blog, 2011 book); not in The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari.

rejected.claim: Sharma: 'The best moment is always the present moment.'
rejected.reason: Not found as a quote in the book.

rejected.claim: 'If you get 1% better every day you will be 37% better in a year.'
rejected.reason: Not in the book (popularized by James Clear, 2018) and mathematically wrong (1.01^365 is about 37.8 times, not 37 percent).

1354.note: Fixed: village of Sivana, not a monastery; fiction stated clearly.

1355.note: Five-regrets list is not in the book; recentered on the book's own deathbed mentality (Divea's hourglass, John's father). Title changes.

1356.note: Recentered on the sumo wrestler and the push-up scene; 1%/37% and Toyota dropped; kaizen origin caveat added.
